questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has 3 months of weight loss, heat intolerance and palpitations. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 134/70 mmHg. She has a fine tremor, warm sweaty palms, a diffuse goitre and brisk reflexes. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised. Her GP looks for an examination finding that would point specifically to Graves' disease as the cause.
questions.q: Which finding is most specific for Graves' disease?
questions.e: Exophthalmos is the most specific sign of Graves' disease; tremor, tachycardia and weight loss occur with any cause of thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Most features show thyrotoxicosis; only some show its cause.

elim: Seen in Graves' but also in Hashimoto's and thyroiditis.
A feature of thyrotoxicosis from any cause.
Seen in any cause of thyrotoxicosis.
Non-specific to the cause.

steps.x: **B. Exophthalmos.** Eye signs = Graves'.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with Graves' disease and proptosis has noticed raised, thickened, orange-peel patches on the front of both lower legs over 2 months. They are not painful or ulcerated. She has no diabetes. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis of her skin lesions?
questions.e: Pretibial myxoedema (thickened, peau d'orange shins) is a sign of Graves' disease, alongside exophthalmos and thyroid acropachy, despite its name.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: orange-peel patches on the front of both lower legs
steps.x: Shin plaques in a patient with Graves'.

elim: Tender red nodules, often with sarcoidosis or streptococcal infection.
Shiny yellow-brown plaques, associated with diabetes, which she does not have.
Painful ulcers with a violaceous edge.
Itchy, scaly skin with varicose veins in older people.

steps.x: **C. Pretibial myxoedema.** Pretibial myxoedema = Graves', not hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with long-standing Graves' disease and severe eye disease has noticed her fingertips have become broad and swollen over a year. She has never smoked and has no cough, bowel symptoms or heart murmur. X-ray of the hands shows periosteal new bone along the phalanges. She also has pretibial skin thickening.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her finger changes?
questions.e: Thyroid acropachy (clubbing with periosteal new bone) occurs in Graves' disease with eye disease and pretibial myxoedema.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Clubbing with the triad of Graves' extrathyroidal signs.

elim: Clubbing with chronic productive cough, which she does not have.
Clubbing with bowel symptoms.
No murmur or cyanosis.
A never-smoker with no respiratory symptoms; Graves' signs explain it.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid acropachy.** Graves' triad: eye disease, pretibial myxoedema, acropachy.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 6 weeks of anxiety, sweating and weight loss. She has a firm, non-tender, diffuse goitre. She had no recent viral illness and is not postpartum. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm. Her eyes are normal. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her thyrotoxicosis?
questions.e: Hashimoto's can start with a transient thyrotoxic phase (hashitoxicosis) with a non-tender goitre and strongly positive TPO antibodies.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Thyrotoxic, painless goitre, TPO positive, TRAb negative.

elim: Painful, tender goitre after a viral illness.
TSH receptor antibodies are negative and there is no eye disease.
A single nodule, not a diffuse goitre.
Nodular goitre in older people.

steps.x: **C. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Hashitoxicosis: TPO positive, painless goitre, transient.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has a routine review after an episode of palpitations. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. She feels well otherwise, with no weight loss or tremor. She takes no thyroid medicines or amiodarone. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Low TSH with normal free T4 and T3 is subclinical hyperthyroidism; it is linked to AF and osteoporosis, and treatment is indicated if AF is present.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: takes no thyroid medicines or amiodarone
steps.x: Suppressed TSH with normal hormones.

elim: Would show a raised free T4 or T3.
TSH would be raised or normal, not suppressed.
Occurs in acute illness, usually with low T3; she is well.
Would show a raised TSH.

steps.x: **D. Subclinical hyperthyroidism.** Low TSH + normal T4 = subclinical hyperthyroidism; treat if AF.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with Graves' disease on carbimazole has 3 days of cough and fever. Today she is agitated and confused, vomiting and has diarrhoea. Her temperature is 40.2°C, pulse rate 164 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 168/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation. She takes no antipsychotics or serotonergic drugs.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right lower zone consolidation: the infection that triggered the storm.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening decompensation of thyrotoxicosis, often triggered by infection, surgery or stopping antithyroid drugs.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hyperpyrexia, delirium, tachyarrhythmia and GI upset in Graves' with an infection.

elim: Follows antipsychotics, with rigidity; she takes none.
Episodic hypertension and headache; does not fit known Graves' with infection.
Infection is the trigger, but hyperpyrexia, agitation and fast AF in Graves' is storm.
Follows serotonergic drugs, with clonus.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid storm.** Graves' + infection + fever + delirium + fast AF = thyroid storm.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has untreated thyrotoxicosis. Over 2 weeks he has become breathless lying flat with swollen ankles. His pulse rate is 140 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 150/60 mmHg, and his hands are warm with a bounding pulse. He has a raised JVP and bibasal crackles. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
questions.e: Excess thyroid hormone increases cardiac output and heart rate; with AF this can cause high-output heart failure.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Heart failure with a hyperdynamic circulation.

elim: Causes a slow-rising pulse and narrow pulse pressure, not a bounding pulse.
No fever; the X-ray shows oedema, not consolidation.
Does not explain warm peripheries and thyrotoxicosis.
Would not give cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema and a bounding pulse.

steps.x: **D. High-output cardiac failure.** Thyrotoxicosis → AF and high-output cardiac failure.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man has 3 months of loose stools 4 times a day, weight loss of 6 kg despite eating more, and feeling on edge. He has no blood in his stools or abdominal pain. He is sweaty and his hands shake. His pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 136/64 mmHg. Tissue transglutaminase antibodies are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Excess thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate and sympathetic activity: weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, anxiety, tremor and sweating.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: weight loss of 6 kg despite eating more
steps.x: Hypermetabolic state with sympathetic overactivity.

elim: Antibody test is negative, and it does not cause tremor and tachycardia.
Usually with abdominal pain, blood or raised inflammatory markers.
Does not cause weight loss with increased appetite.
Does not cause weight loss, tremor and tachycardia.

steps.x: **E. Thyrotoxicosis.** Weight loss + good appetite + tremor = check TFTs.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has had scanty, irregular periods for 4 months. She has lost 4 kg, feels hot and irritable and sleeps badly. Pregnancy test is negative. She has no acne or excess hair. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm. She has a smooth diffuse goitre and lid retraction. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 36 pmol/L (9–25).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her menstrual change?
questions.e: Thyrotoxicosis causes menstrual irregularity; a diffuse goitre and lid retraction in a young woman point to Graves'.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: smooth diffuse goitre and lid retraction
steps.x: Young woman, thyrotoxic, diffuse goitre, eye signs.

elim: Can cause amenorrhoea and weight loss, but not a goitre and raised T4.
No acne or hirsutism and does not cause thyrotoxicosis.
Test is negative.
Causes amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea, not thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **B. Graves' disease.** Menstrual irregularity is a thyrotoxic symptom.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has De Quervain's thyroiditis diagnosed 2 weeks after a flu-like illness. She has a tender goitre, palpitations and sweating. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm. ESR is raised and an isotope scan shows globally reduced uptake. She asks what is most likely to happen over the coming months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely outcome?
questions.e: De Quervain's (subacute) thyroiditis is often post-viral and self-resolving, sometimes with a temporary hypothyroid phase.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Post-viral painful thyroiditis.

elim: Not needed; the condition settles.
The thyrotoxic phase is self-limiting.
A different autoimmune disease; not the expected course.
Arises in Hashimoto's, not De Quervain's.

steps.x: **D. Spontaneous resolution.** De Quervain's resolves on its own; treat symptoms.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has 6 months of palpitations, sweating and weight loss. He has also had headaches and his peripheral vision has narrowed. He has a diffuse goitre. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his thyrotoxicosis?
questions.e: A raised (not suppressed) TSH with high free T4 is secondary hyperthyroidism; with headache and field loss it suggests a pituitary adenoma needing MRI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
TSH inappropriately high with high T4, plus a mass effect.

elim: TSH would be fully suppressed.
Thyrotoxic phase would suppress TSH.
Rare, and does not explain headache and visual field loss.
Autonomous nodules suppress TSH.

steps.x: **E. TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma.** High TSH + high T4 = secondary hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has 2 months of weight loss, palpitations and heat intolerance. Her pulse rate is 114 bpm and BP 132/66 mmHg. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 39 pmol/L (9–25). She has a diffuse goitre and her palms are warm. The examining student is asked to predict a finding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows
questions.e: Thyrotoxic examination: tachycardia, fine tremor, warm moist skin, goitre, hyperreflexia, AF and lid lag.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Clear thyrotoxicosis.

elim: Hypothyroid; thyrotoxicosis gives warm, moist skin.
A hypothyroid sign.
A hypothyroid feature.
Hertoghe's sign, hypothyroid.

steps.x: **A. Brisk reflexes.** Thyrotoxicosis: brisk reflexes; hypothyroid: slow-relaxing.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman delivered a baby 3 months ago. She has 3 weeks of palpitations, irritability and poor sleep. She has a small painless goitre and no eye signs. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 30 pmol/L (9–25). TSH receptor antibodies are negative and isotope uptake is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painless thyrotoxicosis months after delivery with low uptake and negative TRAb is postpartum thyroiditis; its thyrotoxic phase is treated with propranolol.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Painless, low-uptake thyrotoxicosis after pregnancy.

elim: Painful and tender after a viral illness.
TSH receptor antibodies are negative and uptake is low, not diffusely high.
Does not cause raised T4.
Single hot nodule on scan.

steps.x: **D. Postpartum thyroiditis.** Postpartum thyroiditis: low uptake, TRAb negative; propranolol.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 4 months of weight loss, sweating and palpitations. He has a lumpy goitre with several firm nodules of different sizes on both sides. He has no eye signs. His pulse rate is 98 bpm irregular. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 27 pmol/L (9–25). TSH receptor antibodies are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Toxic multinodular goitre (Plummer's disease) is the second commonest cause, typically over 50, with multiple autonomous nodules.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: several firm nodules of different sizes on both sides
steps.x: Older patient, multinodular goitre, antibody negative.

elim: Diffuse smooth goitre with positive TRAb and often eye signs.
Diffuse firm goitre, usually hypothyroid.
A rapidly growing mass, usually hypothyroid.
One nodule, not several on both sides.

steps.x: **E. Toxic multinodular goitre.** Over 50 + many nodules = toxic multinodular goitre.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has 2 months of tremor, sweating and weight loss. His pulse rate is 110 bpm. He has a smooth, symmetrical, diffuse goitre with a bruit over it and bilateral lid retraction. He takes no medicines. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 is 42 pmol/L (9–25) and free T3 is 14 pmol/L (3.5–6.5).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Graves' disease is the commonest cause; antibody-driven stimulation gives a diffuse, vascular goitre (bruit) and eye signs.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: smooth, symmetrical, diffuse goitre with a bruit
steps.x: Diffuse vascular goitre with eye signs.

elim: He takes no medicines.
Painful and tender goitre.
A single nodule, not a diffuse goitre.
Nodular, older patients.

steps.x: **C. Graves' disease.** Diffuse goitre + bruit + eye signs = Graves'.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has 2 months of palpitations, weight loss and tremor. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm. She has a diffuse goitre. Thyroid function tests are sent.
questions.q: Which result is most likely?
questions.e: Primary thyrotoxicosis gives a suppressed TSH with a raised free T4 (± T3).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Overt primary thyrotoxicosis.

elim: Secondary hyperthyroidism, which is rare.
Primary hypothyroidism.
Secondary hypothyroidism.
Subclinical hyperthyroidism; she is clinically overt.

steps.x: **C. TSH low, free T4 high.** Thyrotoxicosis: low TSH, high T4.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman is referred by her GP to the community mental health team with 3 months of anxiety, irritability and poor sleep. The psychiatrist notes she has lost 5 kg, is sweaty and has a fine tremor. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 130/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Thyroid function tests are the first-line and gold-standard test for suspected thyrotoxicosis; anxiety with weight loss and tremor needs them before a psychiatric label.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.

clues: lost 5 kg, is sweaty and has a fine tremor
steps.x: Anxiety with physical hypermetabolic signs.

elim: For phaeochromocytoma, which is far less likely.
Not indicated for anxiety with physical signs.
Used to find the cause after TFTs confirm thyrotoxicosis.
Supports Graves' once thyrotoxicosis is confirmed.

steps.x: **C. Thyroid function tests.** Anxiety + weight loss + tremor: TFTs first.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman has thyrotoxicosis with a TSH of <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 26 pmol/L (9–25). She has an irregular, lumpy goitre and no eye signs. TSH receptor antibodies are negative. A radioisotope thyroid uptake scan is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the scan?
o: Single hot nodule with suppression of the rest
questions.e: Toxic multinodular goitre shows patchy uptake from several autonomous nodules.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Older woman, multinodular, antibody negative.

elim: Graves' disease.
Thyroiditis such as De Quervain's.
Would not fit a thyrotoxic autonomous goitre.
Toxic adenoma.

steps.x: **D. Patchy uptake in multiple nodules.** Patchy = toxic multinodular goitre.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has 2 weeks of a painful neck radiating to his ears, fever and palpitations after a cold. His thyroid is tender. His pulse rate is 104 bpm. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0), free T4 is 31 pmol/L (9–25) and ESR is 72 mm/h. A radioisotope uptake scan is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the scan?
questions.e: In De Quervain's, inflamed follicles leak stored hormone but cannot trap iodine, so uptake is globally reduced.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Painful post-viral thyroiditis.

elim: Graves' disease.
Would not fit thyroiditis with released hormone.
Toxic multinodular goitre.
Toxic adenoma.

steps.x: **B. Globally reduced uptake.** Low uptake = thyroiditis (hormone leak, not overproduction).

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has thyrotoxicosis with a smooth diffuse goitre. TSH receptor antibody results are delayed, and her endocrinologist requests a radioisotope uptake scan to confirm the cause before planning treatment. She is not pregnant or breastfeeding.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the scan if she has Graves' disease?
questions.e: In Graves', antibodies stimulate the whole gland, so isotope uptake is diffusely increased.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Whole-gland stimulation.

elim: Thyroiditis.
Would not fit an overactive gland.
Toxic multinodular goitre.
Toxic adenoma.

steps.x: **A. Diffuse increased uptake.** Diffuse increased = Graves'.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has palpitations and weight loss. TSH is 5.9 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 33 pmol/L (9–25), confirmed on repeat at a different laboratory. She takes no medicines and has no biotin supplements.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A raised rather than suppressed TSH with high free T4 suggests secondary hyperthyroidism, which is investigated with pituitary MRI.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Thyrotoxic with an inappropriately raised TSH.

elim: Used to find a thyroid cause when TSH is suppressed.
For suspicious nodules.
Does not look at the pituitary.
Graves' suppresses TSH; this TSH is raised.

steps.x: **A. MRI of the pituitary.** TSH not suppressed in thyrotoxicosis → pituitary MRI.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman is 10 weeks pregnant. She has palpitations, heat intolerance and a smooth diffuse goitre. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 35 pmol/L (9–25). Her obstetrician wants to confirm the cause without exposing the fetus to radiation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: TSH receptor antibodies support Graves' disease and avoid the radiation of an isotope scan; they also predict fetal thyroid risk.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.

clues: without exposing the fetus to radiation
steps.x: Confirming Graves' when a scan is not allowed.

elim: Uses radiation and does not show function.
Contraindicated in pregnancy.
A marker after thyroid cancer treatment.
Found in Hashimoto's and are less specific for Graves'.

steps.x: **E. TSH receptor antibodies.** Pregnant + thyrotoxic: TRAb, not isotope scan.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with Graves' disease was started on propylthiouracil at 6 weeks of pregnancy. She is now 14 weeks pregnant and her thyroid function is well controlled. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm. Her full blood count is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to her treatment?
questions.e: Propylthiouracil is first-line in the first trimester (carbimazole is contraindicated then); switch to carbimazole in the second and third trimesters.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
She has left the first trimester.

elim: Block-and-replace is avoided in pregnancy.
PTU is used in the first trimester; switch after it because of liver toxicity.
Contraindicated in pregnancy.
She needs ongoing control.

steps.x: **B. Change to carbimazole.** PTU in trimester 1, then carbimazole.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has newly confirmed Graves' disease. She has troublesome palpitations, tremor and anxiety and has no asthma. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 136/70 mmHg. Carbimazole has been started today but she is told it will take several weeks to work.
questions.q: Which drug will most rapidly relieve her symptoms?
questions.e: Propranolol blocks beta-adrenergic effects of thyroid hormone, controlling palpitations and tremor within hours while carbimazole takes effect.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Need rapid control of adrenergic symptoms.

elim: An antiarrhythmic that can itself cause thyroid dysfunction.
Treats anxiety only and not the adrenergic drive.
Would worsen thyrotoxicosis.
Takes months and is not used for symptom control.

steps.x: **D. Propranolol.** Propranolol for symptoms; carbimazole for the thyroid.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has newly diagnosed Graves' disease with no eye disease. She is started on carbimazole and propranolol and asks how long she will need to take the carbimazole before the team considers stopping it or moving to definitive treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate duration of treatment?
questions.e: In Graves', propranolol plus carbimazole is given for 12–18 months while awaiting remission or definitive treatment.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Standard antithyroid course.

elim: Far too short to induce remission.
This is how long until she becomes euthyroid, not a full course.
Antithyroid drugs are not normally lifelong.
Not the measure used to set duration.

steps.x: **A. 12–18 months.** Graves' carbimazole course: 12–18 months.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman has toxic multinodular goitre. She has no compressive symptoms or eye disease. She has taken carbimazole for 8 weeks and is now euthyroid. She lives alone and has no children at home. She wants definitive treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
o: Continue carbimazole for 18 months then stop
questions.e: Radioactive iodine is first-line definitive treatment for toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma, given after 6–8 weeks of antithyroid control.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: no compressive symptoms or eye disease
steps.x: Autonomous nodular disease ready for definitive treatment.

elim: Nodules are autonomous and relapse after stopping.
Symptom control only.
A last resort; for compressive goitre or failed radioiodine.
She is thyrotoxic without treatment.

steps.x: **C. Radioactive iodine.** TMNG/toxic adenoma: radioiodine.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with Graves' disease has a very large goitre. She has noisy breathing when lying flat and difficulty swallowing solids. CT shows the goitre narrowing the trachea. She has relapsed after a course of carbimazole. She is euthyroid on treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
questions.e: Thyroidectomy is used in Graves' for large compressive goitres, relapse, or severe eye disease, despite risks to the parathyroids and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: relapsed after a course of carbimazole
steps.x: A compressive goitre needing removal.

elim: She has relapsed and the goitre is compressive.
Symptom control only.
Can cause transient swelling and is less suitable for a large compressive goitre.
Tracheal compression needs treatment.

steps.x: **D. Total thyroidectomy.** Compressive goitre: thyroidectomy.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease yesterday. She is comfortable and her neck wound is flat and dry. Her voice has become weak and breathy, and she coughs when drinking. Her calcium is 2.31 mmol/L (2.20–2.60).
questions.q: Which complication has she most likely developed?
questions.e: Thyroidectomy risks hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve damage; a hoarse, breathy voice and aspiration point to the nerve.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Voice change and aspiration after thyroidectomy with normal calcium.

elim: Her calcium is normal.
The wound is flat and dry.
No fever, tachycardia or agitation.
Too early and the wound is clean.

steps.x: **C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.** Post-thyroidectomy hoarseness = recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman delivered 4 months ago. She has 3 weeks of palpitations and anxiety. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm. She has a small painless goitre. TSH is suppressed, free T4 is raised, TSH receptor antibodies are negative and uptake is low. She is bottle feeding and has no asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: The thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis is treated with propranolol for symptoms; antithyroid drugs do not help.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Painless postpartum thyroiditis in its thyrotoxic phase.

elim: Ineffective; hormone is leaking, not overproduced.
Not for the thyrotoxic phase.
Used for severe De Quervain's, not postpartum thyroiditis.
Uptake is low and the condition is self-limiting.

steps.x: **D. Propranolol.** Postpartum thyroiditis: propranolol.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has De Quervain's thyroiditis. She has 10 days of a painful, tender thyroid after a viral sore throat, with mild palpitations. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm. Isotope uptake is globally reduced. She has no history of peptic ulcer or asthma.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: De Quervain's is managed supportively with NSAIDs for pain, adding corticosteroids if severe or unrelieved.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Self-limiting painful thyroiditis.

elim: No excess synthesis to block; hormone is leaking from damaged follicles.
Same reason as carbimazole.
Uptake is low and the condition resolves.
Not indicated in a self-limiting condition.

steps.x: **B. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.** De Quervain's: NSAIDs, steroids if severe.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with Graves' disease is brought in confused and agitated after a week of stopping his carbimazole. His temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 158 bpm, BP 150/64 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. He has no asthma. IV access is obtained and fluids are started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Thyroid storm needs admission and aggressive treatment: IV propranolol, an antithyroid drug, corticosteroids and supportive care with fluids.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Thyroid storm with life-threatening tachycardia.

elim: Would worsen the thyrotoxicosis.
Too slow and unsafe in a storm.
Thyroid storm needs admission and aggressive treatment.
Surgery in storm is dangerous; stabilise medically.

steps.x: **A. IV propranolol.** Storm: beta-blocker + antithyroid + steroid + supportive care.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman with thyroid storm has been given IV propranolol, propylthiouracil and IV hydrocortisone, with IV fluids. One hour after the propylthiouracil, the team wants to add a drug that rapidly blocks release of preformed thyroid hormone from the gland.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to add?
questions.e: Potassium iodide inhibits thyroid hormone release and is given after the antithyroid drug in thyroid storm.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: blocks release of preformed thyroid hormone
steps.x: An adjunct that stops hormone being released.

elim: Can worsen thyroid dysfunction.
Already covered by PTU and does not block release.
Would worsen thyrotoxicosis.
Destroys tissue over months; not for emergency use.

steps.x: **D. Potassium iodide.** Storm adjunct: iodide (after the thionamide).

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant presents in thyroid storm. She is being treated with IV propranolol, propylthiouracil, hydrocortisone and IV fluids. The team considers further drugs to control the thyrotoxicosis.
questions.q: Which drug should be avoided?
questions.e: Lithium is a second-line option in thyroid storm but is contraindicated in pregnancy because of the risk of Ebstein's anomaly.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Pregnancy restricts the drug choices.

elim: Blocks T4 to T3 conversion and is part of storm treatment.
Supportive care for a hypermetabolic, vomiting patient.
Used for fever.
First-line antithyroid drug in thyroid storm.

steps.x: **C. Lithium.** Lithium in pregnancy = Ebstein's anomaly risk.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has taken amiodarone for 3 years for recurrent ventricular arrhythmias. He now has weight loss, tremor and worsening palpitations. TSH is <0.01 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 38 pmol/L (9–25). His cardiologist agrees an alternative antiarrhythmic is possible.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction requires drug withdrawal where possible, with cardiology input; it risks AF and high-output heart failure.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Thyrotoxicosis caused by a drug that can be replaced.

elim: Amiodarone is driving the thyrotoxicosis.
Treats hypothyroidism.
Ineffective with the iodine load from amiodarone.
Not the first step.

steps.x: **D. Stop amiodarone.** Amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction: withdraw the drug.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with a history of toxic multinodular goitre has 6 weeks of a hoarse voice. The right side of her goitre has grown quickly and feels hard and fixed. She has a firm lymph node in her right neck. She has not had any surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Hoarseness with an anterior neck mass is a red flag for malignant recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and needs urgent surgical referral.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
A growing hard neck mass with nerve involvement.

elim: Does not address a possible malignancy.
Not before excluding cancer.
Hoarseness with a growing neck mass is a red flag.
Delays assessment of a possible cancer.

steps.x: **A. Fast-track suspected cancer referral.** Neck mass + hoarseness = urgent referral.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with thyroid storm is given IV hydrocortisone in addition to propranolol and propylthiouracil. Her temperature is 39.8°C and pulse rate 150 bpm. Her random cortisol is normal. A student asks why a steroid helps when she has no adrenal problem.
questions.q: Which is the main mechanism of benefit?
o: Blocks conversion of T4 to T3
Inhibition of iodine uptake into the gland
questions.e: Corticosteroids block peripheral conversion of T4 to the more active T3 in thyroid storm.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Each storm drug acts at a different step.

elim: This is propranolol's action.
This is radioactive iodine.
This is propylthiouracil and carbimazole.
Not the steroid effect.

steps.x: **B. Blocks conversion of T4 to T3.** Steroids in storm: block T4 → T3.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has a single 3 cm thyroid nodule, a suppressed TSH and raised free T4. An isotope scan shows intense uptake in the nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland. She has no thyroid antibodies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the nodule's hormone production?
o: Antibody stimulation of the TSH receptor
questions.e: Toxic adenomas and nodules arise from somatic mutations that make them produce hormone autonomously, escaping TSH feedback.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: intense uptake in the nodule with suppression of the rest
steps.x: One autonomous nodule; the rest of the gland is switched off.

elim: Graves'; the whole gland would take up isotope.
Would affect the whole gland.
Thyroiditis gives low uptake.
TSH would be raised, not suppressed.

steps.x: **E. Somatic mutation causing TSH-independent activity.** Hot nodule = somatic mutation, TSH-independent.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man started amiodarone for atrial fibrillation 6 months ago. He now has tiredness, cold intolerance and weight gain. TSH is 18 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 7 pmol/L (9–25).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his thyroid dysfunction?
questions.e: Amiodarone's high iodine content can shut down hormone synthesis (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), causing hypothyroidism; the Jod-Basedow effect causes hyperthyroidism.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Iodine load with an underactive result.

elim: Causes thyrotoxicosis from hormone leak, not hypothyroidism here.
Iodine-driven hyperthyroidism, the opposite of his results.
TSH would be low.
Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism.

steps.x: **E. Wolff-Chaikoff effect.** Wolff-Chaikoff = shutdown (hypo); Jod-Basedow = overdrive (hyper).

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with Graves' disease has a resting pulse rate of 118 bpm, a wide pulse pressure and a hyperdynamic apex beat. A student asks why thyroid hormone excess produces such a strong cardiac effect.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Increased catecholamine secretion from the adrenals
TSH acting directly on the myocardium
questions.e: Excess T3/T4 upregulates beta-adrenergic receptors, increasing heart rate and cardiac output; this explains tachycardia, AF and high-output failure.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Heightened adrenergic sensitivity.

elim: Catecholamine levels are usually normal; it is sensitivity that rises.
Not the mechanism.
Not the mechanism.
TSH is suppressed.

steps.x: **A. Beta-adrenergic receptor upregulation.** Thyroid hormone sensitises the heart to adrenaline.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has thyrotoxicosis with tremor, sweating, anxiety and a pulse rate of 110 bpm. Her plasma catecholamines are normal. Her symptoms improve markedly within a day of starting propranolol, although her free T4 is unchanged.
questions.q: Which best explains her symptoms?
questions.e: Excess thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate and sensitises beta-adrenergic signalling, giving sympathetic overactivity despite normal catecholamines.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: improve markedly within a day of starting propranolol
steps.x: Sympathetic features without excess catecholamines.

elim: Catecholamines are normal.
Causes Cushing's features, not tremor and tachycardia.
Would not persist with normal intake and respond to propranolol.
Her symptoms reflect the raised thyroid hormone.

steps.x: **D. Increased sensitivity to beta-adrenergic stimulation.** Thyrotoxicosis = beta-adrenergic sensitisation.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with Graves' disease has a diffusely enlarged, vascular thyroid. Her TSH is undetectable, yet her gland continues to grow and produce hormone. She asks why the gland keeps working when her pituitary has switched off its signal.
questions.q: Which best explains this?
o: Antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor independently of TSH
Release of stored hormone from damaged follicles
questions.e: IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, driving continuous hormone synthesis and diffuse hyperplasia independent of pituitary feedback.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
A signal other than TSH is driving the gland.

elim: Causes nodular disease, not a diffuse goitre.
Not the mechanism in Graves'.
TSH is undetectable.
Thyroiditis, which does not cause gland growth.

steps.x: **A. Antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor independently of TSH.** Graves' = TSH-independent receptor stimulation.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman is 8 weeks pregnant with newly diagnosed Graves' disease. She is started on propylthiouracil. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and free T4 is 34 pmol/L (9–25). She asks how the tablet reduces her thyroid hormone levels.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of propylthiouracil?
questions.e: Propylthiouracil (like carbimazole) inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking hormone synthesis; it is first-line in the first trimester and in thyroid storm.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Thionamide action.

elim: Propranolol.
No routine drug does this.
Radioactive iodine.
Iodide and lithium.

steps.x: **C. Blocks thyroid peroxidase.** Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase.
